plot: Odo and Mothwick follow the true Strasbourg dancing plague of July 1518: Frau Troffea dances for days without music, strangers join, doctors prescribe more dancing and the council hires musicians and builds a stage; the twist is that the 'cure' spread it, because frightened people believed in Saint Vitus' curse, and it ends only when music is banned and the dancers are taken to the shrine at Saverne.

beats.say: 1518, Strasbourg. One woman stepped into the street and began to dance.
Dance? In the middle of the street? Why didn't she stop?
Her name was Frau Troffea. It was mid July, and very hot.
This one is true, Odo. The city wrote everything down.
Her husband begged her to stop. She danced until she fell.
She slept a little, woke up, and started dancing again.
Maybe she just loved music? Was someone playing for her?
No. There was no music at all. Only her feet on stone.
She danced for about six days. Then strangers joined her.
Remember the word strangers, Odo. Nobody had asked them.
Within a week, more than thirty people were dancing in Strasbourg.
Thirty people dancing without music? That's not a party.
Their feet bled through their shoes. They cried for help, still dancing.
Doctors were called. Their answer was very strange.
This is hot blood. The cure is simple. More dancing.
More dancing? Odo, they wanted to dance the sickness out.
Subscribe for a new true story every day. Now it gets worse.
The city council agreed with the doctors. They built a wooden stage.
Hire musicians. Hire strong men to hold them up. Keep them moving.
Drums and pipes played day and night in the guild halls.
Wait. Music made it better, right? Please say it worked.
It did not. When people saw the music, they joined in.
One chronicle says up to four hundred people danced that summer.
The cure was the thing spreading it. The music called them.
Some dancers collapsed in the heat. Chronicles say some never got up.
Then why didn't they just tie them to their beds?
Nobody knew what it was. So the council changed its mind.
No more music. No drums in the city. The stage comes down.
Gambling and loud music were banned in Strasbourg for weeks.
So the street went quiet. Did the dancing stop too?
Slowly. Wagons took the dancers to a shrine in the hills.
The shrine of Saint Vitus, at Saverne. They were given red shoes.
Red shoes, a prayer, and quiet. By September it was over.
But what was it? A curse? Something in the bread?
Here is the strangest part. Look back at the strangers.
Strasbourg had years of famine, cold winters and new sickness.
People believed Saint Vitus could curse sinners with a dance.
So when they saw one dancer, frightened people feared it was them next.
Historian John Waller calls it mass psychogenic illness. Fear that spreads.
So the music didn't cure them. It told everyone the curse was real.
Doctors and councillors wrote it all down. Their notes still survive.
And Frau Troffea? Nobody wrote down what happened to her.
I'm not tapping my foot, Mothwick. That's just the wind.
If this one got you, the Christmas ghost army of Edgehill is next.
Have you heard a story like this one? Tell me in the comments.

long.title: Summer 1518: A Town That Couldn't Stop Dancing | True Story
long.description:
Previous true story: https://youtu.be/1ntmNRGVkKg
Have you heard a story like this one? Tell me in the comments.

"She danced for six days. Then the city tried to help, and made it worse." — Odo

A true story from Strasbourg, July 1518: Frau Troffea started dancing in the street and could not stop. Within weeks dozens joined her. Doctors prescribed more dancing, the council hired musicians and built a stage, and the crowd grew. Only when music was banned and the dancers were taken to the shrine of Saint Vitus did it end.

Sources:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dancing_plague_of_1518
